body: Managing partner of ValueQuest Capital LLP (New Delhi), adviser to the ValueQuest India Moat Fund; long-time adjunct professor at MDI Gurgaon (behavioural finance and business valuation courses; course details not re-verified here); LSE economics; practising value investor in India for 25+ years. His blog (fundooprofessor) and lectures are among the best Indian writing on moats, Munger-style mental models, 'Lollapalooza' effects and the evolution from Graham-style cheapness to quality. Process edge (as he describes it): buy durable-moat businesses when temporary 'bad news' - regulatory scare, one-off loss, sector panic - pushes the price down, and hold; look for 'clean surprises' (businesses whose hidden strengths show up later in numbers); watch for incentive-caused bias in promoters. Track record: ValueQuest's fund returns are not public in this research - treat any number as unverified. Holdings: specific stock attributions circulating online (e.g., chemical or footwear names) could not be verified and are excluded. Mistakes: he has written about selling great businesses too early and owning cheap-but-poor businesses early in his career (characterisation). Copyable: his framework is entirely public - read the lectures, build a moat checklist (pricing power, switching costs, network effects, cost advantage), and use bad-news events as entry points only when the moat is intact.

title: Sanjay Bakshi - moats, behavioural finance, 'bad news' investing (India)
